html:
The Wayúu, also called Guajiro, are an Indigenous people of the Guajira Peninsula, the dry northern tip of South America shared by Colombia and Venezuela. They speak an Arawakan language and are among the largest Indigenous peoples of both countries.

The rulers of Spanish America never fully conquered them. Soon after contact the Wayúu took up cattle, goats and horses and became herders, and they traded with Dutch, English and other smugglers along the coast, which helped them stay free. They resisted the Spanish, landowners and the Church for centuries.

Wayúu society is built on matrilineal clans, where descent passes through the mother. Disputes between clans are settled by the pütchipü'ü, the "word giver", a mediator whose role UNESCO listed as world heritage in 2010. Wayúu women are known for their woven bags, sold across Colombia. Their land is split by the border, and many move freely across it.
